ABSTRACT
This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to summarize and conclude the clinical evidence
regarding the use of cinnamon among patients with metabolic diseases. A comprehensive litera-
ture search without any limitation on language was conducted using the following bibliographical
databases: ISI Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar. Search was con-
ducted up to 23 January 2020. A total of 35 clinical trials were included for final analysis. Pooling
of results showed a significant reducing effect of cinnamon on total cholesterol (TC) (weighted
mean difference (WMD) ¼/C0 11.67 mg/dL; P ¼ 0.010), triglyceride (TG) (WMD ¼/C0 16.27 mg/dL;
P < 0.001), low density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) (WMD ¼/C0 6.36 mg/dL; P < 0.001), serum glu-
cose (WMD ¼/C0 11.39 mg/dL; P < 0.001), serum insulin (WMD ¼/C0 1.27 lIU/mL; P ¼ 0.028), and waist
circumstance (WC) (WMD ¼/C0 1.68 cm; P ¼ 0.016). These lowering effects on TG, TC, LDL-C, and
serum glucose levels were robust in studies that used cinnamon supplementation dose /C20 1.5 g.
Also, our findings of the present meta-analysis showed that cinnamon supplementation could
have favorable effects on high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C, WMD ¼ 1.35; P ¼ 0.038) as
well as systolic (WMD ¼/C0 3.95 mmHg; P ¼ 0.018) and diastolic (WMD ¼/C0 3.36; P ¼ 0.001) blood
pressure among patients with metabolic diseases. The present meta-analysis suggests that cinna-
mon might exert beneficial effects on various cardiometabolic risk factors among patients with
metabolic diseases.

Introduction
Metabolic diseases are a leading cause of morbidity and
mortality among non-communicable diseases in both devel-
oped and developing countries which affect millions of peo-
ple worldwide each year (Obeidat et al. 2015). The
prevalence of metabolic diseases due to various lifestyle fac-
tors—such as physical inactivity, smoking, and unhealthy
eating habits —have increased dramatically around the world
(Lusis, Attie, and Reue 2008, Obeidat et al. 2015). It is pre-
dicted that by year 2030, the rate of rise is almost 23.6 mil-
lion deaths annually (Watanabe and Kotani 2020). Metabolic
diseases, in addition to having a direct impact on the indi-
vidual, also bear significant cost and burden to the govern-
ment and community (Tang et al. 2017). As a result, it is
important to adopt appropriate strategies for the
management and prevention of metabolic diseases for any
healthcare system.
In this context, lifestyle modification, adherence to a
healthy diet and physical activity, as well as the use of
pharmacotherapy are the most important therapeutic
options for management of metabolic diseases (Alberti et al.,
2009, Xu et al. 2018, Patti et al. 2018, Cicero and Colletti
2016, Cicero, Tartagni, and Ertek 2014, Guo et al. 2020,
Kord-Varkaneh et al. 2020, Fatahi et al. 2018, Meng et al.
2020, Varkaneh Kord et al. 2020, Wang et al. 2020, Fatahi
et al. 2020). However, due to the difficulty of maintaining
long-term lifestyle changes as well as adverse side effects of
medications—such as myopathy and hepatotoxicity —the
number of people who choose plant based-therapies as an
alternative to control metabolic diseases have increased

(Pourmasoumi et al. 2018, Sahebkar 2017). In this regard,
herbs and spices have recently attracted significant attention
in scientific societies and consumers due to their safety,
popularity, ease of access, and reduction in the number of
side effects (Peter 2006). Historically, many herbal medicines
have been administered to prevent and manage risk factors
related to metabolic diseases (Banach et al., 2018, Johnston
et al. 2017, Ma et al. 2017, Wood et al. 2003).
Cinnamon is one of the most common flavorings in the
food industry around the world. It is a spice from
Cinnamomum and the Lauraceae family which is derived
from the inner skin of a tropical evergreen tree (Gruenwald,
Freder, and Armbruester 2010). Cinnamaldehyde, cinnamic
acid, eugenol, and coumarin as main components found in
cinnamon, play key important roles in different biological
activities, such as anti-microbial, anti-inflammatory, antioxi-
dant, antifungal, and anti-diabetic activities (Ranasinghe
et al. 2012, Zaidi et al. 2015).
The protective effects of cinnamon and its constituents
have been investigated in several human trials, and it is
assumed that the anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory prop-
erties of cinnamon might be responsible for these protective
effects (Tuzcu et al. 2017, Hariri and Ghiasvand 2016).
However, the results are controversial in this context. For
example, some researchers have reported beneficial effects of
cinnamon in this framework (Mousavi et al. 2019,
Yazdanpanah et al. 2020), while others did not observe such
effects (Namazi et al. 2019, Maierean et al., 2017). Some
meta-analysis studies examined the effects of cinnamon on
biochemical parameters (Namazi et al. 2019, Yazdanpanah
et al. 2020, Mousavi et al. 2019), however, the effects of cin-
namon on metabolic disorders are not exactly defined,
owing to differences in findings, inclusion criteria, outcomes
of interest, analysis, and health status. Furthermore, for
some of these meta-analysis studies (Allen et al. 2013,
Maierean et al., 2017), the literature search was limited to
2016 and studies published afterward in recent years have
not been included.
Given in this field that no comprehensive review has
been performed, we thus conducted a systematic review and
meta-analysis of all available randomized controlled trials
(RCTs) to provide a precise estimate of the overall effects
and safety of cinnamon among patients with meta-
bolic diseases.
Methods
The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and
Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009) were
followed to perform and report the current meta-analysis.
Search strategy
Relevant articles were identified through five electronic data-
bases including: SCOPUS, EMBASE, PubMed, Web of
Science, and Google Scholar. The literature was searched
from inception until January 2020 without any language
restriction. The following search terms (merge of MeSH and
non-MeSH) were used: Cinnamomum zeylanicum,
Cinnamomum, Cinnamon, Cinnamomum verum, AND
“Intervention Studies ” [Title/Abstract] OR “intervention”
OR [Title/Abstract] “controlled trial ” [Title/Abstract] OR
“randomized” [Title/Abstract] OR “randomised” [Title/
Abstract] OR “randomly” [Title/Abstract] OR “placebo”
[Title/Abstract] OR “assignment” OR “randomized con-
trolled trial ” [Title/Abstract] OR RCT [Title/Abstract] OR
blinded [Title/Abstract] OR “double blind ” [Title/Abstract]
OR ‘controlled clinical trial ’ [Title/Abstract] OR ‘crossover
procedure’ [Title/Abstract] OR “Cross-Over trial ” [Title/
Abstract]. Also, in order to avoid missing any relevant stud-
ies, we manually checked all reference lists of eligible
articles, related reviews, and meta-analyses. The PubMed ’se -
mail alert had been activated to find any new articles in this
field that might be published after our search.
Eligibility criteria
Retrieved studies were included in our review if they met
the following evidence-based PICOS criteria: 1) Patients:
adult individuals /C21 18 years old with metabolic diseases, 2)
Intervention: cinnamon supplementation, 3) Control: pla-
cebo intervention, 4) Outcomes: sufficient data for extrac-
tion about total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), low
density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), high density lipo-
protein-cholesterol (HDL-C), waist circumference, systolic
blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), serum
glucose, serum insulin, serum glycated hemoglobin A1c
(HbA1c), or homeostatic model assessment for insulin
resistance (HOMA-IR), and 5) Study design: RCT.
Excluded studies
Studies were excluded if they: 1) were conducted among
children, pregnant women, or animals, 2) were not placebo-
controlled trials, 3) did not report the targeted outcomes,
(4) investigated the effects of cinnamon in combination with
other components, and (5) were unpublished documents
and gray literature such as conference papers, dissertations,
and patents.
Data extraction
Two independent investigators screened the titles and
abstracts of articles initially retrieved from online search of
databases and extracted all relevant data which were double
checked by other authors. These data included: first author
’s
name, year of publication, country where the study was per-
formed, study design, study period, health status of partici-
pants, total number of sample size, type of intervention, and
the outcomes reported. We also contacted the corresponding
authors of select RCTs to acquire missing data that were not
reported in the articles.

Quality assessment
Two reviewers (SF and FS) independently evaluated the
methodological quality of the eligible studies via the
Cochrane Collaboration ’s tool, version 1 (ROB1). This tool
evaluates 7 domains as follows: 1) random sequence gener-
ation (selection bias); 2) allocation concealment (selection
bias); 3) blinding of participants and personnel (perform-
ance bias); 4) blinding of outcome assessment (detection
bias); 5) incomplete outcome data (attrition bias); 6) select-
ive reporting (reporting bias); and 7) other biases (Higgins
et al., 2011). Three scores of yes, no, and unclear could be
given to each aforementioned item, which were interpreted
as high risk, low risk, and unknown risk, respectively.
Data synthesis and statistical analysis
The statistical analysis was performed using RevMan version
5.3 software and STATA version 12.0 software. If data was
expressed in a different format, standard calculations were
executed to obtain the mean and standard deviation (SD)
(Higgins 2011, Hozo, Djulbegovic, and Hozo 2005). For
instance, if the SD of the change was not stated in the trials,
we derived it using the following formula: SD
change ¼ square root [(SD baseline 2 þ SD final 2) /C0
(2 /C2 R /C2 SD baseline /C2 SD final)]. Also, for trials that only
reported standard error of the mean (SEM), SD was
obtained using the following formula: SD ¼ SEM /C2 /H20881n,
where “n” is the number of subjects in each group.
The degree of statistical heterogeneity between studies was
assessed with the use of the I
2 statistic. We reported statistical
heterogeneity as important if it was at least moderate to sub-
stantial (I
2>50%) or if there was inconsistency across RCTs
in the direction of effect (Higgins et al. 2003). Also, in order
to identify potential sources of heterogeneity, a pre-defined
subgroup analysis based on cinnamon dosage, duration of
supplementation, and health status of subjects was performed.
We pooled outcomes as weighted mean differences (WMD)
with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A sensitivity analysis was
performed to assess the contribution of each study to the
overall WMDs. We assessed the presence of publication bias
using the formal Egger ’s test (Egger et al. 1997).

Meta-analysis results
Effect of cinnamon supplementation on TC levels
Twenty-three studies with 27 arms including a total of 1516
participants (case ¼ 759 and control ¼ 757) reported TC as
an outcome measure. Overall results from the random-effects
model indicated that cinnamon supplementation significantly
reduced TC levels after intervention (WMD ¼ -11.67 mg/dL,
95% CI: /C0 20.56, /C0 2.78, P ¼ 0.010), with significant heterogen-
eity being noted among the studies ( I
2¼94.6%, P < 0.001)
(Figure 2). In the subgroup analysis, we found that cinnamon
supplementation dose and type of disease could explaine this
heterogeneity. Studies that were conducted on cinnamon sup-
plementation dose /C20 1.5 g (WMD ¼/C0 18.36 mg/dL, 95% CI:

Discussion
Metabolic diseases are the main causes of death and disabil-
ity worldwide (Kelly et al. 2017). Consequently, several
nutrition-based therapeutic strategies have been developed
with the aim of improving modifiable risk factors, and pre-
venting the onset of metabolic diseases (Heneghan et al.
2018). Cinnamon, as a potential dietary ingredient with
beneficial health effects against metabolic diseases, has
gained a considerable interest. Therefore, we critically inves-
tigated the scientific evidence regarding its efficacy and
examined a range of factors including insulin, glucose,
HbA1c, SBP, DBP, TG, LDL-C, TC, HDL-C, and WC
in adults.

Our findings from the present meta-analysis showed that
cinnamon supplementation could have favorable effects on
all risk factors associated with metabolic diseases. Indeed,
our results support beneficial effects of cinnamon supple-
mentation on lipid profiles, glycemic status markers, blood
pressure parameters, and waist circumference.
Combined results from the random-effects model indi-
cated that cinnamon supplementation could significantly
reduce TC, LDL, and TG levels, while increase HDL levels.
Also, the stratified analysis indicated that studies that were
conducted on cinnamon supplementation dose /C20 1.5 g and
intervention duration >8 weeks had greater reduction in TC,
LDL-C, and TG levels. Thus, it seems that doses higher than
<1.5 g of cinnamon supplementation are neither appropriate
nor necessary for greater effectiveness as previous reports
had suggested this hypothesis (Mousavi et al. 2019). We also
observed a non-linear dose-response relationship between
dosage of cinnamon supplementation and change of TG and
LDL-C levels. Additionally, the stratified analysis based on
duration of intervention revealed that HDL-C levels further
increased after cinnamon consumption in studies with
intervention duration >8 weeks. In line with our findings, a
systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (Maierean
et al., 2017) showed that cinnamon supplementation indeed
modified the levels of lipid indices and these changes were
further aided by an increase in the duration of intervention.
However, the results for HDL-C and LDL-C levels were not
significant statistically, and this could be ascribed to the
small number of included RCTs compared with our
study (n ¼ 35).
The possible mechanism of cinnamon efficacy on lipid
profile may be attributed to the capacity of cinnamaldehyde
in stimulating lipolysis via activation of AMP-activated pro-
tein kinase (AMPK), leading to inhibition of fatty acid syn-
thesis (Shen et al. 2014). AMPK is involved in the
maintenance of lipid and cholesterol homeostasis and
through phosphorylation inhibits the activity of acetyl-CoA
carboxylase (Shen et al. 2014). Also, cinnamaldehyde with
increased activity of lecithin cholesterol acyl transferase may
also favorably contribute to the regulation of blood lipids,
including evaluating the HDL-C levels (Medagama 2015).

reducing dyslipidemia (Borzoei, Rafraf, and Asghari-

Our results revealed the significant beneficial effects on
various glycemic indices, including glucose, HbA1C,
HOMA-IR, and insulin level after intervention with cinna-
mon. Also, studies with a supplementation duration
>8 weeks and dose /C20 1.5 g cinnamon declared greater reduc-
tion in glucose concentration. Stratified analysis also showed
a significant effect of cinnamon on HbA1C based on dur-
ation of supplementation. However, none of subgroup ana-
lysis reported significant changes in HOMA-IR and serum
insulin levels after cinnamon supplementation. To the best
of our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis that has
examined the effect of cinnamon on insulin levels and
HOMA-IR. However, there are three prior meta-analyses on
the effects of cinnamon on glycemic parameters (Namazi
et al. 2019, Allen et al. 2013). Our results on the effect of
cinnamon supplementation on fasting serum glucose levels
were consistent with previous studied but not for HbA1C
levels. These different findings might be ascribed to differen-
ces in inclusion criteria between both prior meta-analyses
and our study. In other words, we tried to examine the
complementary effects of cinnamon in all patients with
metabolic disorders, in contrast to meta-analyses that had
only been performed on diabetic patients (Allen et al. 2013,
Namazi et al. 2019). Potential mechanisms for anti-diabetic
activities of cinnamon are not well understood. However,
several pathways are suggested. Cinnamtannin B1, a proan-
thocyanidin component extracted from Ceylon cinnamon,
has been depicted to stimulate the phosphorylation of insu-
lin receptor b-subunit on adipocytes and other insulin
receptors, and thus improving insulin sensitivity (Medagama
2015). Also, based on accumulating evidence, cinnamon
extract acts via the AMPK signaling pathway to induce glu-
cose transporter type 4 (GLUT-4) translocation, thereby
facilitating the entry of glucose into the cell, and thus reduc-
ing the serum glucose levels and status of insulin resistance
in the body (Cao, Polansky, and Anderson 2007, Nikzamir
et al. 2014). Furthermore, cinnamon can enhance the

expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated alpha and
gamma (PPAR- a and PPAR- c), and thus can increase insu-
lin sensitivity (Kopp et al. 2014). Furthermore, in diabetic
rats, the pyruvate kinase (PK) activity, a key enzyme
involved in the regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism,
was decreased after treatment with cinnamon (Anand
et al. 2010).
The present analysis showed that cinnamon had a lower-
ing effect on SBP and DBP. Also, subgroup analysis indi-
cated that longer supplementation can lead to greater
reduction in SBP and DBP. In addition, the dose-response
analysis showed that the results were independent of the
dosage of cinnamon. This null observation for the latter
finding might be due to the fact that the dosages of studies
were nearly similar. Based on our results, cinnamon supple-
mentation significantly reduced the levels of SBP and DBP,
and thus cinnamon supplementation could be used as an
effective adjunct therapy with conventional anti-hypertensive
agents in clinical practice. Evidence from literature showed
that even 2 mmHg reduction in SBP and DBP could reduce
mortality from ischemic heart disease and stroke by 7% and
10%, respectively (Khalesi et al. 2014, Lewington et al.
2003). Thus, the favorable lowering effects of cinnamon con-
sumption on SBP and DBP may have important public
health and cardiovascular benefits. Numerous lines of
research disclosed that cinnamon, as a powerful anti-oxidant
ingredient, could reduce oxidative stress by neutralizing
active oxygen species, thereby improving the production and
bioavailability of nitric oxide (NO), a molecule with vaso-
dilatory properties (Mollazadeh and Hosseinzadeh 2016).
Studies also displayed that cinnamon has antagonistic cal-
cium activity and could affect vascular endothelial vessels,
thereby modulating blood pressure (Schiffrin 2010, Shen
et al. 2012). In addition, owing to the high potassium con-
tent of cinnamon, one study reported that cinnamon could
potentially increase sodium excretion and reduce the con-
traction of arterial smooth muscles, subsequently leading to
lower blood pressure (Filippini et al. 2017).
Our summary results indicated that cinnamon could
decrease WC and it might be helpful in reducing abdominal
obesity or visceral fat. Similarly, a recent systematic review
and meta-analysis reported that cinnamon supplementation
reduced WC, but this change was not statistically significant
(Namazi et al. 2019). UCP3 gene plays a pivotal role in fatty
acid metabolism as well as carbohydrate and lipid oxidation
(Akilen et al. 2010). UCP3 gene expression has been shown
to be increased following cinnamon supplementation, which
may secondarily affects WC changes (Akilen et al. 2010).
Furthermore, according to previous research, cinnamon par-
ticipates in energy metabolism and delays gastric emptying
(Namazi et al. 2019). All in all, cinnamon may indirectly
participate in reducing the WC.
Based on the abovementioned findings, cinnamon can
have potentially beneficial effects on various cardiometabolic
risk factors. With regard to toxicological profile, cinnamon
is generally considered safe by the United States Food and
Drug Administration and no serious side effects have been
reported in studies. However, only one article reported mild,
short-lived gastric upset and headache after administration
(Akilen et al. 2010). Also, caution should be exercised with
high doses of cinnamon ( >10 grams per day), as previous
reports indicated potential side effects, such as burning, ten-
derness, increased heart rate, and liver problems
(Hajimonfarednejad et al. 2018). Furthermore, individuals
taking anticoagulant agents should consult physicians before

Our meta-analysis has some strengths. To the best of our
knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis and dose-response
study of RCTs evaluating the impact of cinnamon supplemen-
tation among patients with metabolic diseases. In addition,
since our study only involved RCTs, the causal inference of
our findings is strong. Nonetheless, our study has limitations
that ought to be acknowledged. First, the effect of some con-
founding factors such as dietary intake and physical activity
were not considered in most of the studies. Second, the hetero-
geneity of the overall results was high in terms of condition,
dosage, and duration, which might have affected the efficacy of
the results. Nevertheless, we tried to identify some possible
sources of heterogeneity by performing subgroup analysis and
we were largely successful.
Conclusion
The current meta-analysis on available RCTs suggested that
cinnamon might have beneficial effects on lipid profiles, gly-
cemic status markers, waist circumference, and blood pres-
sure parameters in patients with metabolic diseases. Also,
subgroup analysis indicated that longer supplementation of
cinnamon could lead to greater change in lipid profile,
blood pressure, as well as serum glucose and HbA1c levels.
Moreover, the lowering effects of cinnamon on TG, TC,
LDL-C, and glucose were robust in studies that were con-
ducted with cinnamon supplementation dose /C20 1.5 g. In con-
sideration of the overall safety of cinnamon and its
popularity as common food ingredient, cinnamon may be
used in combination with standard of care pharmacological
agents to promote enhanced management of various
